# Why Tip Screens Often Start Higher Than You Planned

You finish your meal, tap your card, and the screen turns to one final question:

“Would you like to leave a tip?”

Under that question are several suggested amounts. The first choices may be much higher than the amount you had in mind.

This is not only a feeling. A 2014 study by Kareem Haggag and Giovanni Paci examined more than 13 million credit-card taxi payments in New York City. The researchers found a useful natural comparison. Around a $15 fare, the suggested tip menu suddenly changed. So they could compare almost identical rides that showed different suggested rates.

Passengers who happened to see the higher suggested rates usually left more money. In other words, the first number on the screen can become a starting point for the customer’s decision.

But there is a catch.

When the suggested rate was set too high, some passengers did not simply choose a smaller custom amount. They left no credit-card tip at all.

That creates a strange result. A higher number can bring in more money from some customers, but it can also push other customers away from tipping completely.

The same question is now appearing far beyond taxis. Restaurants, cafés, delivery services, and other businesses use digital payment screens that place the tip decision directly in front of the customer.

## From a quiet tip jar to a public decision

Michael Lahr of Rutgers University’s New Jersey State Policy Lab says the social setting has changed. In the past, a cash tip jar allowed people to decide more privately. On a digital screen, an employee may be standing nearby while the customer chooses a percentage.

That can create what Lahr calls “guilt tipping.” The customer is not only asking, “What do I want to pay?” They may also be asking, “What will this person think if I choose the lowest option?”

The suggested rates have also moved upward over time. Lahr’s 2022 policy brief says restaurant tipping in the United States rose from about 10 to 15 percent in the early 1970s to about 20 percent by the late 1990s. Today, some digital screens show tips as high as 35 percent.

## Customers are starting to push back

That pressure may be losing its power. In a Popmenu consumer survey released in April 2026, 78 percent of respondents said tipping had become ridiculous, and 44 percent said they had reduced their tips from the year before.

The survey also found that 36 percent preferred to enter a custom amount instead of choosing a suggested rate. Still, 59 percent said a digital prompt made them feel they should leave a tip, down from 66 percent in September 2025.

The numbers do not prove that tip screens caused these changes. But they show growing fatigue with the system—and a stronger wish to make the final choice personally.

## In one line…

A tip screen is not just asking for money; it is setting the opening number in a social moment. Set that number too high, and it may produce not generosity, but resistance.

# The Tip Screen Keeps Asking for More

You finish your meal, turn the card machine toward yourself, and there they are: 20 percent, 25 percent, sometimes even 35 percent.

You were planning to leave less. But now the screen has given you a new starting point.

That small design choice can change the final payment. A peer-reviewed study by Kareem Haggag and Giovanni Paci, published in 2014, examined more than 13 million credit-card taxi rides in New York City.

The researchers noticed something useful. For fares just below and just above $15, the screen suddenly showed different suggested tip menus. The rides were very similar, but some passengers saw higher starting rates than others.

Passengers who happened to see the higher suggestions left more money. This showed that the first percentage on the screen could strongly influence the final tip.

But there was a twist.

When the suggested rates became too high, some customers did not simply choose a smaller amount. They chose zero and paid no credit-card tip at all.

A policy brief by Michael Lahr of Rutgers University’s New Jersey State Policy Lab presents this as part of the business logic behind digital tipping. A higher starting point may bring in more money, without much measurable effect on customer satisfaction or return visits.

So the screen is doing more than recording a decision. It is helping set the terms of the decision.

### From a private jar to a public choice

Lahr writes that restaurant tipping in the United States rose from about 10 to 15 percent in the early 1970s to about 20 percent by the late 1990s. Today, digital screens can show tips as high as 35 percent.

With a cash tip jar, the choice was relatively private. With a screen, the employee may be standing right in front of the customer. That can create pressure at the exact moment the percentage is chosen—a feeling Lahr calls “guilt tipping.”

### Customers are starting to push back

A Popmenu consumer survey released on April 8, 2026, found that 78 percent of respondents thought tipping had become ridiculous. Forty-four percent said they had reduced their tips compared with the year before.

The pressure has not disappeared, but it may be weakening. The share who felt they had to leave a tip when prompted by a digital screen fell from 66 percent in September 2025 to 59 percent in 2026. And 36 percent said they chose a custom amount instead of the suggested rates.

These are self-reported survey results, so they do not prove that the screens caused the change. But they show a clear mood: many customers are no longer willing to treat the first number as the right number.

## In one line…

The tip screen sets the starting line—and when that line moves too far, customers may not pay more; they may walk away from tipping altogether.
